Abstract: We reexamine the empirical “square-root law” of market impact, which describes a concave relationship between size of institutional orders and average price response. I argue that this pattern can arise as a statistical artefact rather than a structural feature of price formation.

###### Abstract
The square-root impact law (SRIL), I≃Yσ(√(Q/V)), bundles two facts that a single mechanism must explain at once: a *shape* (impact proportional to square-root of traded volume Q) and an *amplitude* (Y=O(1), independent of the participation rate φ). ## (1) Introduction
In Bonart (2026a), I have proposed a framework that rejects this invariance assumption. The starting point is simple: prices are structurally diffusive. This means that in mature and liquid markets, persistent return predictability attracts arbitrage and is progressively eliminated. A sufficiently persistent change in trading behavior should therefore trigger an adaptive market response. Following this argument, it turns out that the impact law of a trader must depend on the statistics of that trader’s order flow (Bonart, 2026a).
Square-root impact need therefore not reflect an anomalous response mechanism (Bouchaud et al., 2006). It can arise as a by-product of diffusivity. This picture also changes the interpretation of optimal execution and price manipulation arguments. A fixed impact law may admit a cost-minimizing or apparently price-manipulating strategy, while that strategy may itself move the market outside the regime over which the impact law remains invariant. The opportunity and the model that generates it can therefore be mutually inconsistent. The impact law becomes a moving target.
## (3) Review of the existing framework
Bonart (2026a) derives restrictions on market impact from a single structural requirement: prices are diffusive both with and without the trader. The argument does not ask how primitive impact is generated. It asks instead which impact processes are compatible with arbitraged prices, and it finds that the answer is strongly constrained.
What is assumed is that the “equilibration time” needed for arbitrage to become effective is short enough so that impact measurements on typical observational datasets operate de facto under the stationary regime. # Diffusive in plain sight: An inconspicuous law of market impact
Julius F. Bonart

###### Abstract

Decomposing impact as the difference between realized and counterfactual returns and requiring both to be diffusive yields an identity that restricts admissible impact scaling at the level of individual participants. This constraint implies the square-root law in the information-neutral regime and a crossover to linear impact under strong informational coupling, consistent with empirical observations. In the weak-coupling regime, cumulative market impact is itself diffusive – a diagnostic that many propagator and latent liquidity models fail to satisfy.
The square-root law has often been regarded as anomalous (Bouchaud et al., 2006; Mastromatteo et al., 2014). Our approach suggests rather the opposite: square-root impact is not anomalous but a direct consequence of price diffusivity, independent of specific assumptions about aggregate demand and supply dynamics.
## (5) Consequences of the structural constraint
Eq. (2.2), Eq. (3.1) and Eq. (4.2) impose non-trivial constraints on how impact scales with trading activity. Under mild and empirically relevant assumptions, these constraints imply a diffusive impact in an information-neutral setting, a square-root scaling in duration, a linear-to-square-root crossover of impact as a function of trading rate and informational alpha and, consequently, the empirical square-root law of metaorder impact.
## (8) Conclusion
This constraint nearly fixes the admissible scaling structure of market impact. In the absence of informational coupling, impact increments must be effectively uncorrelated, independently of aggregate supply and demand dynamics. Information-neutral impact is therefore diffusive. Conversely, a square-root-to-linear crossover is predicted to occur when information content starts to dominate mechanical impact. Our framework thus recovers the empirical phenomenology.

Title: On the origin of nonlinear market impact: Statistical conditioning and artefactual concavity

Abstract: We reexamine the empirical “square-root law” of market impact, which describes a concave relationship between size of institutional orders and average price response. I argue that this pattern can arise as a statistical artefact rather than a structural feature of price formation. Under minimal assumptions—mean-reverting trading signal, rational expectations pricing, and statistical independence between order duration and participation rate—the conditional drift of prices during execution follows a square-root scaling as a consequence of the Doob h-transform. This result holds across alternative economic interpretations, including informational (Kyle-type) and mechanical (order-flow anticipation) frameworks, both of which yield linear price-formation equations. The analysis suggests that the observed concavity of market impact may reflect conditioning bias rather than genuine nonlinearity. This reinterpretation has implications for transaction cost analysis, causal inference in market microstructure, and challenges the empirical foundation of recent claims that markets are intrinsically unstable or self-organized near criticality.

# On Bonart's interpretation of the Square-Root Impact Law

The square-root impact law (SRIL),
I=YσQ/V, bundles two facts that a single mechanism must explain at once: a shape (impact proportional to square-root of traded volume Q) and an amplitude (Y=O(1), independent of the participation rate φ). Bonart has recently proposed an elegant solution: if realized and counterfactual prices are both diffusive, information-neutral impact must have white increments and the SRIL follows without the wart. We reformulate and simplify his argument, and foreground the ingredient he himself regards as essential --- that the market whitens the stationary stream of each participant's metaorders, not any isolated one. The Lillo--Mike--Farmer model satisfies his premises, yet gives an isolated metaorder the super-square-root impact φ(1−γ)/2Q(1+γ)/2, γ∈(0,1), because single metaorders (i.e. not part of a stream) are statistically invisible and thus priced mechanically. We then construct an explicit multi-agent propagator that realizes Bonart's whitening, and show it reproduces the clean SRIL precisely when the market can attribute trades to their issuer. But correct re-attribution of anonymous trades is a formidable task, which requires markets to behave as implausibly efficient signal processing machines. The stream hypothesis makes a sharp, falsifiable prediction --- isolated metaorders, well separated in time, should not obey the SRIL --- that does not seem agree with empirical data known to us. Independently, a volume-conservation argument singles out the square-root law and lays bare the step the diffusivity route must assume: diffusivity fixes the variance of impact --- an additive, stationary, age-blind quantity --- whereas the SRIL is a law for the mean impact, which marginally decays as 1/age and therefore demands an origin of time.

Square-root market impact may be (almost) a tautology. Prices move like a random walk. That basic fact turns out to quietly dictate one of the most famous empirical laws in finance: the so-called square-root law. Trade X times more and you move the price (on average!) not X times more, but roughly √X more. Still, what is strange: Why are there so many competing approaches? Why are we still so unsure about the basic origin of market impact? Impact is the difference between what actually happened (realized returns) and what would have happened without your trade (counterfactual returns). Keep the square-root law in your cost model, but give price diffusivity less credit for it. Bouchaud, Mastromatteo and Tóth make a convincing case through algebra. keenable.title: Diffusive in plain sight: An inconspicuous law of market impact
keenable.snippet:
Decomposing market impact as the difference between realized and counterfactual
returns, and requiring both to be diffusive, yields a structural identity that restricts
admissible impact dynamics at the level of individual participants. This constraint
implies the square-root law in the information-neutral regime and a crossover toward
linear impact under strong informational coupling, consistent with empirical obser-
vations. It further implies that impact must adapt to each participant’s order-flow
statistics, with consequences for theories of optimal execution and no-arbitrage. In the
information-neutral regime, cumulative impact is itself diffusive, providing a diagnostic
that many propagator and latent-liquidity models fail to satisfy. Under this regime,
market impact retains an undetermined all-pass degree of freedom that prevents its
reduction to a pure surprise model. This residual freedom accommodates transient
impact dynamics and can generate strictly positive impact costs.

Two regimes
emerge. When trading is uncorrelated with underlying price movements – the information-
neutral regime – diffusivity forces impact increments to be effectively white, implying square-
root scaling of its typical magnitude. When trading is instead aligned with underlying
returns, impact grows linearly with volume.

The square-root law has often been regarded as anomalous [Bouchaud et al., 2006, Mas-
tromatteo et al., 2014]. Our approach suggests rather the opposite: square-root impact is not
anomalous but a direct consequence of price diffusivity, independent of specific assumptions
about aggregate demand and supply dynamics. More precisely, when trading is uncorrelated
with underlying price movements, impact itself must be diffusive – a structural requirement
that models based on exogenous, universal kernels generally violate, raising the possibility
that many propagator and latent liquidity models mischaracterize market impact.

keenable-realtime.title: Diffusive in plain sight: An inconspicuous law of market impact
keenable-realtime.snippet:
Decomposing market impact as the difference between realized and counterfactual
returns, and requiring both to be diffusive, yields a structural identity that restricts
admissible impact dynamics at the level of individual participants. This constraint
implies the square-root law in the information-neutral regime and a crossover toward
linear impact under strong informational coupling, consistent with empirical obser-
vations. It further implies that impact must adapt to each participant’s order-flow
statistics, with consequences for theories of optimal execution and no-arbitrage. In the
information-neutral regime, cumulative impact is itself diffusive, providing a diagnostic
that many propagator and latent-liquidity models fail to satisfy. Under this regime,
market impact retains an undetermined all-pass degree of freedom that prevents its
reduction to a pure surprise model. This residual freedom accommodates transient
impact dynamics and can generate strictly positive impact costs.

Two regimes
emerge. When trading is uncorrelated with underlying price movements – the information-
neutral regime – diffusivity forces impact increments to be effectively white, implying square-
root scaling of its typical magnitude. When trading is instead aligned with underlying
returns, impact grows linearly with volume.

The square-root law has often been regarded as anomalous [Bouchaud et al., 2006, Mas-
tromatteo et al., 2014]. Our approach suggests rather the opposite: square-root impact is not
anomalous but a direct consequence of price diffusivity, independent of specific assumptions
about aggregate demand and supply dynamics. More precisely, when trading is uncorrelated
with underlying price movements, impact itself must be diffusive – a structural requirement
that models based on exogenous, universal kernels generally violate, raising the possibility
that many propagator and latent liquidity models mischaracterize market impact.

## AI Overview  
A familiar puzzle sits at the center of market microstructure. Traders often buy or sell in persistent runs, split across minutes or days, which might seem to make prices predictable. Yet prices are broadly diffusive: roughly uncorrelated across time, with variance growing in proportion to elapsed time. Bonart's move is to compare the realized price with the counterfactual price that would have prevailed without a given strategy, and to require both to be diffusive. The Square-Root Law of Market Impact

Dec 01, 2024
(Published by JP Bouchaud | November 2024)

The square-root law for price impact is arguably one of the most fascinating robust empirical regularities discovered in the last 30 years. It states that when executing a buy (sell) “metaorder” of total size Q, sliced and diced into N child orders of size q=Q/N, the price on average moves up (down) by an amount proportional to sqrt(Q).

So far this series has tested Bonart's diffusive theory of market impact on Hyperliquid and extended it to a slow satellite of faster venues:

- The square-root law holds once measured properly, and the √ sits in the number of child orders (Part 1).

- Impact accumulates during your fills, drift accumulates between them, and impact decays faster when an external price anchors it (Part 2).

- Part of HL's measured impact is the primary venue's move that HL hasn't absorbed yet (Part 3).

One assumption remains. In Bonart's framework the market adapts to the *statistics* of order flow, not to the identity of whoever sends it. On most venues that holds, because flow is anonymous.

The counterfactual drift in the model splits into two terms:

> **drift ≈ β × (the primary's not-yet-absorbed move) + α_w**

The first term is lead-lag (Part 3). The second, α_w, is what wallet w knows. Public identities add a third possible term: market makers moving prices in response to *who* is trading, γ·E[α | w]. - **W3.** *Prediction:* Prices react to a wallet's track record beyond what its trades carry (the identity term)

seltz.snippet:
**Market impact models** estimate how much the price of an asset moves *because of your own trading*. For any strategy that trades more than a trivial size, impact is usually the largest single component of transaction cost — larger than commissions and often larger than the bid-ask spread — and it is the main reason a backtest with a 2.0 Sharpe ratio can deliver 0.8 live. This article defines market impact, walks through the three classical model families (linear Almgren-Chriss, the square-root law, and transient propagators), explains why recent research reframes impact as a *causal* quantity that machine learning can estimate, and closes with practical rules for using impact models in algo trading.

## Table of Contents

## What Is Market Impact?

Market impact is the difference between the price path observed while an order is executed and the price path that *would have occurred had the order never been sent*. Formally, for a parent order of QQ shares executed over [0,T][0, T], impact at time tt is

I(t)=E[Pt∣trade]−E[Pt∣no trade].I(t) = \mathbb{E}\left[P_t \mid \text{trade}\right] - \mathbb{E}\left[P_t \mid \text{no trade}\right].

The second term is a counterfactual: it can never be observed directly. Everything that makes impact modeling hard follows from that single fact. Practitioners therefore split impact into two parts. **Temporary impact** is the premium paid to consume liquidity right now and decays once trading stops. **Permanent impact** is the part of the move that persists, usually interpreted as information the market infers from the order flow.

seltz.snippet:
A linear market-impact model makes estimated impact proportional to order size relative to a defined market-volume measure. A square-root model makes it proportional to the square root of that fraction, usually with volatility and fitted coefficients. ## Liquidity Risk Measurement: Quantitative Foundations

If you are a risk quant aspirant, you have probably met liquidity risk as a list of definitions: market liquidity, funding liquidity, bid-ask spreads, survival horizons. That is a fine start, and What Is Liquidity Risk? covers it well. This post is about the next layer down: how liquidity risk is actually *measured*, and why the measurement is a trade-off rather than a lookup.

The central question is simple. You hold a position that is large relative to what the market trades each day, and you have to get out. Sell fast and your own selling pushes the price against you. Sell slowly and the price has more time to move against you anyway. Somewhere between "now" and "never" is a horizon that balances the two, and with two standard building blocks (the square-root law of price impact and the variance of a shrinking position) you can find it with one line of calculus. We will derive it, compute it for six position sizes, and then turn to the other half of the subject: funding liquidity, measured as the number of days a bank survives a run.

**Market liquidity** is how much it costs to turn an asset into cash quickly. **Funding liquidity** is whether you can meet your cash obligations as they fall due. seltz.snippet:
**Market impact** is the price move caused by your own trading. Market impact models estimate it from order size, the asset's volatility and its trading volume, and are used to forecast trading costs, design execution algorithms and judge how much capital a strategy can run.

Market impact models separate permanent impact, the price move that remains because the trade carried information, from temporary impact that decays once trading stops. Empirically, impact rises roughly with the square root of size and about a third to two-thirds decays. Stylised.

### Temporary and permanent impact

- **Temporary impact** is the cost of demanding liquidity now: buying lifts the price through the order book, and this part fades once the buying stops.
- **Permanent impact** is the part that stays, because other participants read the trading as information. In Kyle's (1985) model the price moves by λ per unit of net order flow; λ (“Kyle's lambda”) is a standard measure of illiquidity.

Impact has a mechanical source (consuming resting orders) and an informational one (market makers protecting themselves against informed traders, as in Glosten and Milgrom, 1985). In data the two are hard to separate.

### The square-root law

Across stocks, futures and other markets, the price impact of a large order executed in pieces (a *metaorder*) grows roughly with the square root of its size:

```
Impact ≈ Y × σ × √(Q / V)
σ = daily volatility     Q = order size     V = daily volume
Y = constant of order 1, estimated from data
```

**Example.** A stock with 2% daily volatility trades 1,000,000 shares a day. Buying 100,000 shares (10% of daily volume) with Y = 1 moves the price by about 2% × √0.1 ≈ **0.63%**. Buying 200,000 shares moves it about 2% × √0.2 ≈ 0.89% — double the size, about 1.4 times the impact per share. The total cost (impact × size) therefore rises roughly with Q1.5, which is why capacity limits strategies.

**The square-root impact law** is the empirical observation that the expected price impact of a metaorder grows roughly with the square root of its participation in daily volume, rather than linearly with shares traded. A common form is

\[ I(Q) = Y\,\sigma\,\left(\frac{|Q|}{V}\right)^\delta, \qquad \delta \approx \tfrac12, \]

where \(Q\) is signed parent quantity, \(V\) is relevant market volume, \(\sigma\) is a volatility scale, and \(Y\) is a dimensionless coefficient. This formula is central to capacity planning because it says that doubling assets does not merely double cost.

It is a conditional empirical regularity, not a law of mechanics. Its usefulness comes from expressing impact in normalized units across instruments and regimes; its danger comes from treating a noisy average as a guaranteed price path.

## Why concavity matters

If impact were linear, two equal halves of a parent order would incur the same total expected impact as one whole order under fixed conditions. With square-root impact, the marginal cost declines with completed quantity:

\[ \frac{dI}{dQ} \propto Q^{-1/2}. \]

That does not mean traders should rush the first shares. Volatility, information leakage, temporary liquidity, and benchmark risk change during execution. The formula describes aggregate displacement associated with a metaorder, not a complete optimal schedule.

**Transaction costs are what you actually pay to turn a portfolio on paper into a portfolio you own.** They are the gap between the price you see on the screen and the price you get filled at, plus the fees on top. ultimate.title: On Bonart’s interpretation of the Square-Root Impact Law
ultimate.snippet:
The square-root impact law (SRIL), ℐ≃Yσ√(Q/V), bundles two facts that a single mechanism must explain at once: a *shape* (impact proportional to square-root of traded volume Q) and an *amplitude* (Y=O(1), independent of the participation rate φ). Fixed-kernel models reproduce the shape but carry a “√(φ) wart,” Y∝√(φ). Bonart has recently proposed an elegant escape [3]: if realized and counterfactual prices are both diffusive, information-neutral impact must have white increments and the SRIL follows without the wart. We reformulate and simplify his argument, and foreground the ingredient he himself regards as essential — that the market whitens the stationary *stream* of each participant’s metaorders, not any isolated one. A solvable linear model (Lillo–Mike–Farmer) satisfies his premises, yet gives an *isolated* metaorder the super-square-root impact φ^((1−γ)/2)Q^((1+γ)/2), γ∈(0,1), because single metaorders (i.e. not part of a stream) are statistically invisible and thus priced mechanically. We then construct an explicit multi-agent propagator that realizes Bonart’s whitening, and show it reproduces the clean SRIL precisely when the market can attribute trades to their issuer.

Bonart’s proposal elegantly avoids the wart and correctly predicts a φ-independent prefactor, by replacing the fixed mechanical kernel with the requirement that impact accumulate *diffusively*.

Note that Bonart’s argument also immediately explains why the impact profile of a metaorder is also a square-root, since one only has to replace n_k in Eq. (7) by n_k^((t)), i.e. the number of orders executed up to t, with n_k^((t=N))=n_k. Hence, without any additional assumption, both the peak impact and the running impact obey the square-root law, as empirically observed [7, 22].

Bonart has recently proposed an elegant solution: if realized and counterfactual prices are both diffusive, information-neutral impact must have white increments and the SRIL follows without the wart. We reformulate and simplify his argument, and foreground the ingredient he himself regards as essential --- that the market whitens the stationary stream of each participant's metaorders, not any isolated one. The Lillo--Mike--Farmer model satisfies his premises, yet gives an isolated metaorder the super-square-root impact $\varphi^{(1-\gamma)/2}Q^{(1+\gamma)/2}$, $\gamma\in(0,1)$, because single metaorders (i.e. not part of a stream) are statistically invisible and thus priced mechanically. We then construct an explicit multi-agent propagator that realizes Bonart's whitening, and show it reproduces the clean SRIL precisely when the market can attribute trades to their issuer. But correct re-attribution of anonymous trades is a formidable task, which requires markets to behave as implausibly efficient signal processing machines. The stream hypothesis makes a sharp, falsifiable prediction --- isolated metaorders, well separated in time, should not obey the SRIL --- that does not seem agree with empirical data known to us. Independently, a volume-conservation argument singles out the square-root law and lays bare the step the diffusivity route must assume: diffusivity fixes the variance of impact --- an additive, stationary, age-blind quantity --- whereas the SRIL is a law for the mean impact, which marginally decays as $1/\sqrt{\text{age}}$ and therefore demands an origin of time.

Now comes, in our view, Bonart’s crucial assumption that __the average impact of the metaorder is of the same order of magnitude as the standard deviation__ computed above. This is far from a trivial statement — indeed, the case of a standard zero-drift random walk shows that such a conflation cannot hold in general; Sec. 3 exhibits a solvable impact model in which the two differ completely, and Sec. 6 elaborates the point further.
Granting it for the moment, we get that the impact of metaorder $k$ when the market executes $N$ trades is given by:
$$I(n_{k},N)\propto\varepsilon_{k}\sqrt{b^{2}s^{2}n_{k}},$$
where $\varepsilon_{k}$ is the sign of the metaorder. Nothing in Bonart’s construction fixes this sign and this is actually the crux of the problem, but let us accept fixing it to the direction of the metaorder.
Now, in our simplified setting where all trades are of the same size $q=1$, one has $|Q_{k}|=qn_{k}=n_{k}$ and $V=qN=N$. Now, since $\Sigma_{N}^{2}\propto Ns^{2}$, one can rewrite Eq. (7) as $I(n_{k},N)\propto\Sigma_{N}\sqrt{|Q_{k}|/V}$ or, rewriting in real time, the standard SRIL laid bare:
$$\mathcal{I}\big|_{\rm metaorder}\;\propto\;\sign(Q)\,\sigma\sqrt{\frac{|Q|}{V}}\,,$$
independently of $\varphi$, i.e. without the “wart”: the $\sqrt{\varphi}$ that plagues the fixed-kernel models is here absent because the participation rate $n_{k}/N$ and the duration combine into the total volume, $\varphi\,T\propto Q$, so that $\varphi$ enters only through $Q$. The elegance is undeniable. The rest of this note asks what it entails.
Note that Bonart’s argument also immediately explains why the impact profile of a metaorder is also a square-root, since one only has to replace $n_{k}$ in Eq. (7) by $n_{k}^{(t)}$, i.e. the number of orders executed up to $t$, with $n_{k}^{(t=N)}=n_{k}$. Hence, without any additional assumption, both the peak impact and the running impact obey the square-root law, as empirically observed [7, 22].

ultimate.title: On Bonart's interpretation of the Square-Root Impact Law
ultimate.snippet: The square-root impact law (SRIL), $I = Y\sigma\sqrt{Q/V}$, bundles two facts that a single mechanism must explain at once: a shape (impact proportional to square-root of traded volume $Q$) and an amplitude ($Y=O(1)$, independent of the participation rate $\varphi$). Bonart has recently proposed an elegant solution: if realized and counterfactual prices are both diffusive, information-neutral impact must have white increments and the SRIL follows without the wart. We reformulate and simplify his argument, and foreground the ingredient he himself regards as essential --- that the market whitens the stationary stream of each participant's metaorders, not any isolated one. The Lillo--Mike--Farmer model satisfies his premises, yet gives an isolated metaorder the super-square-root impact $\varphi^{(1-\gamma)/2}Q^{(1+\gamma)/2}$, $\gamma\in(0,1)$, because single metaorders (i.e. not part of a stream) are statistically invisible and thus priced mechanically. We then construct an explicit multi-agent propagator that realizes Bonart's whitening, and show it reproduces the clean SRIL precisely when the market can attribute trades to their issuer. But correct re-attribution of anonymous trades is a formidable task, which requires markets to behave as implausibly efficient signal processing machines. The stream hypothesis makes a sharp, falsifiable prediction --- isolated metaorders, well separated in time, should not obey the SRIL --- that does not seem agree with empirical data known to us. Independently, a volume-conservation argument singles out the square-root law and lays bare the step the diffusivity route must assume: diffusivity fixes the variance of impact --- an additive, stationary, age-blind quantity --- whereas the SRIL is a law for the mean impact, which marginally decays as $1/\sqrt{\text{age}}$ and therefore demands an origin of time.

ultimate.title: Diffusive in plain sight: An inconspicuous law of market impact
ultimate.snippet:
Decomposing market impact as the difference between realized and counterfactual
returns, and requiring both to be diffusive, yields a structural identity that restricts
admissible impact dynamics at the level of individual participants. This constraint
implies the square-root law in the information-neutral regime and a crossover toward
linear impact under strong informational coupling, consistent with empirical obser-
vations. It further implies that impact must adapt to each participant’s order-flow
statistics, with consequences for theories of optimal execution and no-arbitrage. In the
information-neutral regime, cumulative impact is itself diffusive, providing a diagnostic
that many propagator and latent-liquidity models fail to satisfy. Under this regime,
market impact retains an undetermined all-pass degree of freedom that prevents its
reduction to a pure surprise model. This residual freedom accommodates transient
impact dynamics and can generate strictly positive impact costs.

Two regimes
emerge. When trading is uncorrelated with underlying price movements – the information-
neutral regime – diffusivity forces impact increments to be effectively white, implying square-
root scaling of its typical magnitude. When trading is instead aligned with underlying
returns, impact grows linearly with volume.

The square-root law has often been regarded as anomalous [Bouchaud et al., 2006, Mas-
tromatteo et al., 2014]. Our approach suggests rather the opposite: square-root impact is not
anomalous but a direct consequence of price diffusivity, independent of specific assumptions
about aggregate demand and supply dynamics. More precisely, when trading is uncorrelated
with underlying price movements, impact itself must be diffusive – a structural requirement
that models based on exogenous, universal kernels generally violate, raising the possibility
that many propagator and latent liquidity models mischaracterize market impact.

# On Bonart’s interpretation of the Square-Root Impact Law
Bouchaud et al.
The diffusivity argument for square-root impact holds only if markets whiten each trader’s metaorder flow; otherwise impact grows faster.

The square-root law states that the price impact of a large order grows with the square root of its size. A recent argument by Bonart derives it from the diffusivity of prices.
Bouchaud and co-authors show that this derivation only works if markets whiten each participant’s stream of metaorders. Without that condition, isolated metaorders show impact that grows faster than the square root.
The origin of one of the most robust empirical laws of market microstructure therefore remains unsettled.

The diffusive principle (Bonart, 2026). Write the realized price return during your trading as ... The counterfactual is what the price would have done if you hadn't traded. Arbitrage keeps returns close to serially uncorrelated (otherwise someone would trade on the autocorrelation). If your trading carries no information about the counterfactual, impact increments must themselves be uncorrelated, so cumulative impact diffuses like a random walk: it grows like √(number of child orders), which is √(Q/V) when child orders have typical size.
If your trading does predict the counterfactual, the constraint is satisfied differently and impact can grow faster, up to linearly. So Bonart predicts when √ holds (information-neutral flow), what replaces it (faster growth for informed flow), that the √ is really in the number of child orders, and that impact increments should be uncorrelated for uninformed traders.
